transcript.content: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, yeah, nice to meet you too. I guess... well, I'm here because my wife and my director at work basically insisted. It’s hard to explain without giving you the whole backstory, but essentially, I just can’t seem to stop launching projects. And I don't mean just picking up a small hobby here and there. I'm an IT manager, so I'm used to managing complex systems and pipelines, but lately it’s like my brain is just generating a hundred massive tasks at once and I feel this absolute need to execute all of them right this second. 

I'll be drafting these incredibly dense, multi-phase strategic work plans for my department, and then right in the middle of that, I'll decide I need to aggressively accelerate my own professional development. So I'll start mapping out these insane certification schedules, trying to figure out how to knock out three high-level cybersecurity certs in a single month. 

But it doesn't stop at work, it bleeds into my personal life, too. I started completely overhauling our home network—and I mean literally ripping into the drywall to run new Cat6a cable, setting up a full server rack in the basement, configuring enterprise-grade firewalls for a standard suburban house. And while I'm in the middle of configuring all that, I'm suddenly firing off dozens of messages to old contacts on LinkedIn, guys I haven't talked to since my undergrad days, pitching them these massive collaborative ventures and consulting ideas. 

It just... it gets so intense, you know? This drive to just do, do, do. I completely blow past any normal limits of what a person can actually handle, and I don't even realize how far I've pushed it until my wife has to physically step in and pull me away from the basement wiring, or my director pulls me into a private meeting to tell me I'm overwhelming the entire division and need to step back. So... yeah, I guess I'm here because I can't seem to find the off switch, and they're getting worried about it.
Have you been hearing or seeing things that other people don't?

Well, it's funny you ask that, because... I mean, I wouldn't call it "hearing things" in the way people usually mean, like some horror movie or whatever. But, yes, lately there have been these moments. It usually happens when I'm around the equipment. You know, servers have this very specific, constant hum—especially the rack I just set up in the basement, it's got these high-RPM cooling fans that just drone on and on. And when I'm down there, or even just sitting in my home office late at night when the house is totally quiet except for the electronics, I'll start hearing things in the white noise. 

At first, I thought it was just my brain trying to make sense of the sound, like audio pareidolia or something, you know? But it’s gotten more distinct. I'll hear my name, just very clearly, like someone is standing right behind my left shoulder trying to get my attention. And then sometimes it's short phrases. I'll be staring at a terminal window, and I'll hear this voice—it sounds almost mechanical, or maybe just muffled by the fan noise—saying things like, "check the logs." Which, you know, makes sense because I'm an IT guy, I'm always checking logs, but it's not *me* thinking it, it's something I'm actually hearing with my ears. 

And then... well, then there are the other times, when it says things like, "they know." And that one really throws me off. I'll just be running cables or configuring a port, and I'll hear "they know," and I have to stop and physically look around the basement, even though I know my wife is asleep upstairs and there's absolutely no one else in the house. I even checked the security cameras the first few times it happened, thinking maybe I was picking up interference on the baby monitor we use for the dog, or maybe someone was outside near the basement window. But the feeds are always empty. It's just me, the servers, and these... comments coming out of the hum. It's incredibly distracting when I'm trying to execute these massive project phases, let me tell you.
Do you ever hear those voices when your mood and energy feel normal?

Well, it's interesting you phrase it that way, because I've actually been trying to track my baseline lately to figure out exactly that. And the short answer is yes, absolutely. There have definitely been these... I guess you could call them calm or flat stretches. Like, I'll go for a few weeks at a time where I'm not staying up all night running cables or feeling that massive, driving urge to overhaul the entire IT department. I'm just waking up, drinking my coffee, logging in, and feeling pretty average. Not especially up, and definitely not depressed, either. Just... you know, normal. 

But the weird thing is, even during those perfectly average weeks, the stuff I was just telling you about doesn't totally go away. I'll be sitting there in my office, totally relaxed, not stressed at all, and I'll still hear those brief comments when I know for an absolute fact no one is in the room with me. 

And it actually bleeds into other things during those calm periods, too. Like, I'll be looking at my Microsoft Teams dashboard—because as a manager, I have to monitor the presence indicators for my division, you know, green for available, yellow for away, red for busy, the standard stuff. And I'll be sitting there, completely flat energy-wise, but I will still firmly believe that the way people are toggling their statuses are actually coded warnings being sent to me. Like, if three specific developers switch to 'Do Not Disturb' at the exact same minute, it's not a coincidence, it's a very specific signal about a threat. So... yeah, even when my energy is totally leveled out and I'm not on one of those massive project kicks, that stuff is still just happening right there in the background.
Have you been using stimulants like methamphetamine, cocaine, or non-prescribed ADHD medications?

No, no, definitely not. I mean, I get why you'd ask that, given everything I just told you about the energy levels and the staying up all night running cables and all that. It sounds exactly like someone who's hopped up on Adderall or, you know, something stronger. But honestly, I don't touch any of that stuff. Never have. 

I don't even like taking Sudafed when I have a cold because it makes my heart race, you know? And as for illegal stuff, I mean, I work in IT management. We have random drug screenings, and I have high-level security clearances for some of the government contracts my company handles. I can't risk my entire career for something like that. Plus, I don't need it. That's the crazy part. My brain just... does it on its own. It's like I have a built-in overclocking mechanism that just kicks in without any chemical help. 

The most I do is coffee. I mean, I drink a fair amount of coffee, maybe three or four cups a day, usually a dark roast, sometimes an espresso if I'm really dragging in the afternoon, but that's just standard IT fuel. Everyone in my department practically lives on caffeine. But as far as actual stimulants, prescription or otherwise, no, absolutely not. It's just me and my own brain running at a million miles an hour.
Have you had any recent medical or neurological illness or injury, such as a head injury, seizure, stroke, thyroid problem, or brain infection?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I try to keep pretty close tabs on my physical health, all things considered. I get a physical every year, usually around October before the end-of-year crunch at work starts, because once Q4 hits, it's just non-stop server migrations and budget meetings, and I barely have time to breathe, let alone go to a clinic. But no, my bloodwork always comes back totally fine. My thyroid levels, my cholesterol—well, the cholesterol was a tiny bit elevated a few years ago, but I switched to oat milk in my coffee and that pretty much took care of it. 

But as far as anything major, like a head injury or a stroke? No, definitely not. I mean, the closest I've come to a head injury recently was maybe bumping my head on a low-hanging duct in the basement when I was running some Cat6 cable last month. But that was just a scrape, barely even bruised. I didn't black out or get a concussion or anything. And seizures or brain infections? Nothing like that. I haven't even had the flu in like five years. 

I do sometimes wonder, though, if the lack of sleep during those really intense project phases messes with my neurology somehow, you know? Because when you're awake for 48, 72 hours straight, your brain just feels... well, it feels like it's vibrating. But that's not an injury or an illness, that's just... well, that's just the overclocking I was talking about. So, no, physically, neurologically, I'm completely fine. It's just the mental stuff that's... doing whatever it's doing.
Has there ever been a time when the voices or coded-warning beliefs lasted for at least two weeks while your mood was completely normal?

Well, yeah, actually, like I was mentioning earlier when we were talking about tracking my baseline. It's funny you ask it exactly like that, with the two-week timeframe, because I've actually paid really close attention to this lately. And yes, absolutely. There have been several of these... I guess you could call them flat stretches. 

Like, there was this one period last quarter, right before the big Q3 review, where I was just totally level for a good three, maybe three and a half weeks. I wasn't staying up all night, I wasn't feeling that massive drive to just tear apart the server racks and rebuild them from scratch, and I definitely wasn't feeling down or sluggish either. I was just... normal. Waking up at 6:30, making my dark roast, driving to the office, doing my job, coming home, watching a little TV, going to sleep. Completely average mood, completely average energy.

But even during those three weeks, the stuff with the Teams statuses didn't stop at all. I'd be sitting there at my desk, totally calm, maybe sipping my coffee, and I'd look at the dashboard and see that three of my senior network engineers had switched to 'Away' at the exact same millisecond. And I just knew, with absolute certainty, that they were signaling me about a breach or some kind of internal threat that they couldn't put in an email. It wasn't a paranoid panic, it was just a fact to me, even though my mood was totally fine. 

And the voices, too—the brief comments. Like, during that same three-week stretch, I'd be in the server room, which is totally soundproofed by the way, just doing routine cable management. No stress, no crazy energy. And I'd still hear someone right behind my left shoulder say something like, "Check the secondary line," or just a quick, sharp whisper of my name. And I'd turn around, and of course, no one is there. The biometric lock on the door hadn't even engaged. So, yeah, those things definitely persist for weeks at a time, even when my mood is completely, one hundred percent normal. It's like they're running on a completely separate operating system from my emotions, if that makes sense.
